steps.chapter: The bishop line and the question

steps.prompt: Write your move for White and the black piece or pawn you aim at.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The bishop move 7...Bf5 develops with a purpose, yet it leaves the bishop on a square White can attack. How does White try to use that, how should Black answer each try, and which tempting replies lose at once? By the end you can count the guards of g4, find the safe king move after the knight check, and name three traps. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.caption: What does the bishop on f5 attack? Name the squares yourself: c2, e6, g4 and more. Which of them matters most for White's plans?

claims.statement: The bishop on f5 attacks exactly these squares.

steps.text: **What the bishop gives and costs.** [I] On f5 it guards the pawn square e6 and eyes c2, so Black keeps the extra piece developed in one move. The price: the bishop stands where a pawn can hit it. Whoever wants to attack it needs only one thing, a pawn on g4 that cannot simply be taken. Count the guards of g4 before judging.

steps.caption: Count the defenders of g4 now. Black attacks the square twice (bishop and knight); count White's defenders, then answer the question that follows.

claims.statement: Two black pieces attack g4: the bishop and the knight.
No white piece defends g4 while the knight stands on f3.

steps.caption: The knight check changes the count. The knight leaves f3 with check, so the queen's diagonal opens and the knight itself guards g4. Count again.

claims.statement: Now two white pieces defend g4: the queen and the knight.
Two black pieces attack g4.

steps.text: **One move, two jobs.** [I] The knight check forces the king to move, and it opens the queen's diagonal, so g4 is suddenly a playable pawn move. A check that also changes a count is worth more than a check alone. Black's answer must therefore deal with the check and keep the g4 idea in mind.

steps.text: **Why the knight block is better than the pawn block.** [I] With ...Nd5 the e-pawn stays flexible, and nothing ties the bishop on f5 to the defence of e6. With ...e6 the bishop must guard e6 forever, so the moment it is attacked it cannot move. [H] Watch for a pawn that depends on one piece which can be attacked with tempo (here g4 hits the bishop on f5).

steps.title: Does the knight check win the bishop?
steps.prompt: Count the attackers and defenders of the bishop's square in each position, then predict whether the knight check wins the bishop. Only the bishop's square changes. Need an example first? Step back to the fork board, then predict.

steps.text: **Check plus attack is not always a fork.** [I] Before you call a knight check a fork, count the defenders of the attacked piece: the g4 bishop is outnumbered, the d7 bishop is not. [H] Players who learn the fork as a picture, not as a count, fall for it both ways.

steps.text: **Same bishop move, different king and pawn.** [V] With the king on g8 and the pawn on e6, Bxe6+ is mate, so ...Bh7 loses there. With the king on e8 and the pawn still on e7 there is nothing to capture on e6, so ...Bh7 is best; ...Bg6 loses to the knight capture. [I] Do not store 'Bh7 is good' or 'Bh7 loses': ask which pieces stand on e6, e7 and the king's square.

steps.text: **Recap.** [V] After 7...Bf5 the knight check opens the queen's diagonal, so g4 gets two defenders. After the check the king goes to g8 or e8, never e6. After the bishop check the knight block keeps the edge; the pawn block allows g4. When the bishop leaves f5, e6 can fall with check. A check that attacks a piece is only a fork if you win the count.

**Self-check.** Did you say: why g4 was impossible before the knight moved and possible after; the counts on g4 (two against two); why the king goes to g8 and not e6; what the discovered check looks like and why it wins; why ...Bh7 is mate in one; why the knight block beats the pawn block? If one is missing, step through that board again.
